title: SLO Stewardship & Capacity Quiet Mode Playbook
author: Asha Patel
body:
Overview:

Purpose: This playbook defines the "Quiet Mode" pattern — a tightly-scoped operational posture used to protect user-facing SLOs and stabilize capacity during rapid SLO burn or systemic capacity stress. Quiet Mode is a temporary operating state that reduces load, applies routing and quality controls, and centralizes decision-making until normal telemetry demonstrates recovery.

Audience: SRE oncall, service owners, platform routing, and incident commanders.

Scope:
- Applies to multi-tenant inference services and API front doors where rapid error-budget depletion risks user-visible degradation.
- Not intended for full disaster recovery (see cross-cluster failover runbooks).

When to use Quiet Mode:
- Automatic triggers (recommended):
  1) Observed rolling 15m burn rate > 5x SLO expected burn and remaining error budget < 10% for a critical SLO (see Thresholds table).
  2) Aggregate per-cluster CPU/GPU saturation > 90% sustained for 5m and autoscale unable to provision additional capacity.
  3) p99 latency regression > 2x baseline with correlated increase in queue length and tail latency alarms.
- Manual triggers (escalation path):
  - Product/incident commander may request Quiet Mode when customers report systemic failures and the oncall judge determines immediate load control is required.

Roles & responsibilities:
- Oncall SRE (Executor): assess triggers, execute Quiet Mode procedure, coordinate routing changes, and run mitigation checklist.
- Service Owner: approve customer-impacting mitigations, validate rollout decisions, and lead post-event review.
- Platform Routing Team: implement rate limits, priority gates and temporary route policies.
- Observability Owner: confirm telemetry fidelity (ingestion, retention, and dashboard health).

Quiet Mode objectives (in order):
1) Stop further rapid SLO burn.
2) Preserve critical requests and reduce non-critical workload.
3) Stabilize capacity and restore healthy tail latency and error rates.
4) Minimize customer impact by preserving high-priority tenants and API routes.

Quiet Mode thresholds (reference):
| Metric | Trigger | Action Category |
|---|---:|---|
| SLO burn rate (15m) | >5x baseline and error budget <10% | Enter Quiet Mode 
| Cluster GPU utilization | >90% sustained 5m | Enter Quiet Mode / capacity hedging
| p99 latency | >2x baseline | Investigate + throttle low priority traffic
| Error rate (5m) | >3x baseline and increasing | Consider Quiet Mode |

Quiet Mode procedure (step-by-step):
1) Triage (0-5 minutes):
   - Confirm alerts and check related dashboards: SLO portfolio, per-tenant quota, autoscale, and cluster health.
   - Capture hypothesis and note relevant runbook IDs.
   - Announce intent in #incidents with the subject: "Quiet Mode proposed for SERVICE - reason" and tag: @incident-commander, @service-owner. Use template (below).
2) Execute protective controls (5-20 minutes):
   - Apply immediate global rate limit to non-authenticated/experimental routes: default -> 20 RPS per IP or 10% of prior traffic, whichever is lower.
   - Activate priority gating: mark critical routes (e.g., /v1/generate, /v1/chat) as high priority; demote low-value routes (batch embedding jobs, non-essential telemetry requests) to background queue.
   - Enable autoscale emergency policy: allow provisioning of burst nodes without commit checks.
   - Deploy temporary model-fallback policies: route large-context or heavy models to smaller context variants when available.
   - If applicable, toggle caching aggressiveness (prefix/KV) to reduce token recompute.
3) Observe and iterate (20-60 minutes):
   - Monitor SLO burn rate, tail latency, queue length, and eviction rate.
   - If metrics improve and burn rate falls < 2x baseline for 30m, prepare rollback of Quiet Mode.
   - If no improvement, escalate to regional lead and consider capacity rebalancing, tenant evacuation, or emergency provisioning.
4) Exit Quiet Mode (criteria & steps):
   - Exit criteria: sustained SLO burn rate <1.2x baseline for 30m, cluster utilization <80%, and no new correlated errors.
   - Steps: lift rate limits incrementally (30% -> 60% -> full), demote priority gating, revert autoscale emergency policy, and restore regular routing. Notify stakeholders.

Communication templates:
- Initial announcement (Slack):
  "Oncall: proposing Quiet Mode for SERVICE due to [reason]. Triggers observed: [list]. Executing protective controls: global rate-limit, priority gating, emergency autoscale. Owners: @SERVICE_OWNER, @PLATFORM_TEAM. Will update in 15m."
- Customer-facing (support template):
  "We are temporarily operating in a reduced-capacity mode to stabilize API performance for customers. We are prioritizing critical requests and expect restoration within X–Y minutes. We will follow up with a post-event summary."

Runbook command snippets (examples):
- Apply global rate limit (cli):
  rctl apply --service SERVICE --policy global-rate --limit 20rps --scope non-critical
- Mark route priority: (routing API)
  curl -X POST $ROUTER_API/routes/priority -d '{"route":"/v1/generate","priority":"high"}'
- Emergency autoscale toggle (infra):
  infra-cli autoscale set --service SERVICE --policy emergency-burst --approve

Observability checklist (must verify before exit):
- SLO burn rate dashboard: ingestion healthy, no dropouts.
- Token-level traces for a sample of requests: tail latency below threshold.
- Error taxonomy: majority attributable to resource contention vs model regressions.
- Alert fatigue: ensure duplicate alerts suppressed and routed to incident channel.

Post-Quiet Mode review & incident standards:
1) Evidence capture: export 15m/1h/6h windows of relevant metrics (burn rate, per-tenant QPS, queue length, autoscale events, pod evictions). Store artifacts in incident evidence bucket with link in postmortem.
2) Post-incident artifacts:
   - Timeline of actions and exact commands used to enter/exit Quiet Mode.
   - Decision log: who approved each customer-impacting mitigation.
   - Root cause hypothesis and experiment plan for remediation.
3) Postmortem requirements (minimum):
   - One-line summary, impact estimate (requests/minutes and affected tenants), timeline, technical root cause, corrective actions, and owner for each action with ETA.
   - SLO policy updates if trigger thresholds or automation need tuning.

Automation & tooling recommendations:
- Implement Quiet Mode as a composable automation task in the incident runbook runner (e.g., house-runbooks) so protective controls can be applied with a single verified command, while still requiring manual approval for customer-impacting fallbacks.
- Add synthetic canaries that exercise high-cost model routes to detect tail latency increases earlier than aggregate SLOs.
- Enhance token-level sampling to identify tenants that contribute most to burn when Quiet Mode is engaged and support targeted throttling rather than broad cuts.

Metrics & dashboards to monitor (minimum set):
- Portfolio SLO burn rate (1m, 15m, 1h) per critical SLO.
- Per-cluster GPU/CPU utilization and queue length.
- Per-route p50/p95/p99 latency and error-rate.
- Tenant-level QPS and error-rate for top 20 tenants.
- Autoscale events and provisioning latency.

Safety & customer impact guidance:
- Prefer targeted tenant throttles over global cuts when possible.
- Document and track any customer exceptions granted during Quiet Mode.
- All customer-impacting changes require explicit service-owner signoff.

Appendix A — Example thresholds (tunable):
- Critical SLO (availability p99): burn rate >5x and error budget <10% -> Quiet Mode recommended.
- Non-critical SLO: burn rate >10x -> consider selective throttling.

Appendix B — Incident evidence export commands:
1) export_metrics --service SERVICE --metrics burn_rate,p99_latency,queue_length --window 6h --output s3://incidents/SERVICE/2026-03-02
2) snapshot_pods --label service=SERVICE --output /tmp/service_pod_snapshot.json

References:
- See: SLA & SLO portfolio (link to SLO catalog page).
- See related runbooks: tenant-slo-migration-safe-drain, cross-cluster-failover-execution.
